analysis.title: Real Estate Securities Market Review, Third Quarter 2026
key_insights: Global listed real estate fell in 3Q26. The FTSE EPRA NAREIT Developed Index declined about 6% as a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields outweighed resilient property fundamentals.
Regional returns diverged. North America was down about 6.4%, Europe -9.2% (weakest), and Asia Pacific about -3.5%, with Hong Kong the only strong gainer.
The U.S. REIT market fell 6.3% in the quarter against a 2.5% gain for the S&P 500. REITs now lag the S&P 500 by roughly 300 bps year to date, despite being up 10.5%.

The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield rose 80 bps in the quarter to levels not seen in nearly two decades. PGIM expects higher market cap rates across all property types, and the size and duration of that repricing is the key debate for the rest of 2026.

Sectors that depend on external spread investing (buying properties at cap rates above their cost of capital) were penalized most. Sectors with above-average organic growth held up better, and PGIM expects this split to guide REIT sector allocation while rates stay elevated.

Net lease and gaming REITs were the worst U.S. sectors. Both have long lease terms and acquisition-driven growth, and gaming REITs were also hit by tenant rent coverage concerns and a weaker regional casino outlook.
Healthcare and hotel REITs were the best U.S. sectors. Healthcare fell just 1% with Welltower up 1.7%, and hotel RevPAR trends tracked ahead of expectations.
U.S. labor data softened. September nonfarm payrolls rose just 29,000 and unemployment rose to 4.2%. Real personal spending rose 0.6% in August, the fastest monthly pace in over a year.
U.S. capital markets activity was heavy: CSquare (CSQR) IPO in July (4th REIT IPO this year), AVB/EQR and IRT/CSR apartment REIT M&A, Prologis buying SEGRO, and a Brookfield take-private of LXP.

PGIM stays constructive on U.S. REITs over 12 months. It is overweight senior housing healthcare REITs (favoring mid-caps) and data centers, is adding to cold storage, has cut net lease, and has added manufactured housing.

Europe returned -9.2% in 3Q26 (USD gross total return) and -9.4% year to date, against North America at 9.2% and Asia Pacific at -7.4% year to date. The UK was best at -1.4%, helped by Prologis bids for SEGRO, while Spain (-20%) and Germany (-21%) were worst.

Germany was hurt by climbing bond yields and regulation threats to large multifamily residential names. Spain was hit by turmoil in the data center sector affecting its largest stock. France lost ground as French spreads over German bonds widened.

The ECB has delivered two 25 basis point hikes and the Bank of England is expected to start tightening soon. PGIM is cautious on European leverage and maturities, underweight offices, and moderately underweight Europe overall, while preferring industrial/logistics, healthcare and retail.
Europe's public real estate shares trade at significant discounts to private market values, which is drawing M&A interest from midcaps up to large caps.

10-year U.S. Treasury yields peaked at about 5.3%, the highest in 25 years, triggering the Asia Pacific selloff. The market is also wary of further Fed tightening, and a 25 bps Fed hike occurred in September.

Japan developers fell 5.5% in 3Q26 after a 7.5% decline in 2Q. Fundamentals are strong (Tokyo central office rents up 10-20% on lease reversions), and PGIM expects the big two developers to announce earnings upgrades and buybacks with 2Q26 results in November.
JREITs fell 4.1%, a third straight quarterly decline. The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% on 18 September, the 10-year JGB yield moved above 3%, and consensus expects tightening into 2027.

Australian real estate equities fell about 9%. The 10-year Australian yield hit 5.40% near 15-year highs. NextDC fell about 22% in September after a A$1.1bn convertible issue, while Ingenia rallied more than 30% on Warburg Pincus takeover interest.
Hong Kong real estate rose about 6%. Wharf REIC rallied more than 40% after raising its payout ratio from 65% to 90%, and SHKP underperformed on weak results.
Singapore REITs returned -5.0% and developers -4.3% in local currency, against STI +11.2%. CDL fell 11.2% and Suntec REIT 8.9% after strategic reviews disappointed.

In Asia Pacific PGIM is overweight Japanese developers, underweight JREITs, overweight Australian retail REITs and data center developers, and prefers industrial and data center SREITs and Hong Kong companies with shareholder return initiatives.

Near-term direction depends on inflation, monetary policy and sovereign bond yields. PGIM remains constructive over 12 months and favors high-quality, low-leverage names with organic growth, while staying cautious on leveraged and acquisition-dependent companies.

market_movers.rationale: Welltower, the largest healthcare REIT, rose 1.7% in 3Q26 while the sector fell 1%. PGIM is overweight senior housing REITs.

sector_views.rationale: Low supply and strong demographic demand should drive sector-leading NOI and earnings growth, and new capital may limit cap rate expansion.
Unprecedented compute demand and limited power availability.
PGIM believes demand has troughed after years of weak fundamentals, and sees significant upside from depressed valuations. It continues to add.
Above-average growth and reasonable valuation. PGIM added to the sector.
A more challenging acquisition environment. PGIM lowered its weight.
Higher vacancy in secondary locations, substantial capex backlogs and the potential for further private market value adjustments.
Structural growth and predictable, growing income streams.
Positive office and condo fundamentals and improving shareholder returns.
Preference toward large-cap office and residential sectors.
Beneficiaries of domestic consumption and a favorable demand-supply balance.

sector_views.sector: Singapore industrial and data center REITs

earnings_insights: Mitsubishi Estate reiterated its 9% ROE target for the fiscal year in its 1QFY26 results, helped by overseas capital gains, Tokyo office leasing and Tokyo condo sales.
Mitsui Fudosan came in slightly below consensus on 1QFY26 results (reported) due to slower domestic asset sales bookings. Management said this would be largely secured by the 2Q26 results.
PGIM says consensus is forming that the big two Japanese developers will announce earnings upgrades and additional buybacks with 2Q26 results in November (expectation, not yet reported).
Invincible Investment set a medium-term target of at least 3% annual DPU growth. Japan Hotel REIT raised its DPS outlook.
Nippon Building Fund and Japan Prime Realty raised medium-term earnings and distribution growth targets.
SHKP reported weaker-than-expected results and outlook, and Henderson Land performed well following results.
Advance Residence reported rent increases of close to 19% on tenant turnover. Activia and Daiwa Office REIT achieved double-digit rent increases on renewals.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Yield reached levels not seen in nearly two decades, pressuring REIT valuations and raising expected cap rates.
Highest in 25 years, which triggered a selloff in Asia Pacific real estate equities.
Labor market fatigue. A softer labor market could help REITs if inflation fears ease and yields retrace.
Rising, consistent with a moderating labor market.
Fastest monthly pace in over a year, showing a resilient consumer.
Raised on 18 September, and consensus expects tightening to extend into 2027.
Near 15-year highs. A softer-than-expected monthly CPI print moderated RBA hike expectations.
Market wary of further Fed tightening with inflation elevated.
ECB has begun tightening, raising borrowing costs for leveraged European real estate.

risk_factors: Further rise in sovereign bond yields and higher cap rates, which would cut property values.
Higher leverage and borrowing costs in Europe, with a pause in transaction markets and erosion of cash flows.
Acquisition-dependent growth models and highly leveraged companies in a high-rate environment.
Gaming REIT tenant rent coverage and a weaker regional casino outlook.
Data center capital requirements and regulatory pressure causing share-price volatility.
Rising inflation fears, AI capex debt load and U.S. fiscal concerns.
Further Fed tightening and BoJ, RBA and Bank of England tightening.
Weaker residential markets in Australia, where home values are 5.2% below their March peak, and in Hong Kong.
geopolitical: Political risks from upcoming elections in Spain and France, and French macropolitical concerns that widened French spreads over German bonds.
Regulation threats in Spanish data centers and German multifamily residential.
Rising world energy prices, to which Europe is more exposed through net imports.
Upcoming U.S. mid-term elections and implications for U.S. foreign policy and geopolitical uncertainty.
Mainland China tighter outbound-investment controls and offshore income tax enforcement weighing on Hong Kong property demand.
U.S. fiscal concerns and Australia's Tier 1 chip export status under the U.S. framework.

tension_points.bull_case: Operating fundamentals are strong: low new supply, steady occupier demand and positive earnings revisions. If the rate surge proves temporary, the selloff is an attractive entry into a sector with multi-year support.
tension_points.bear_case: The 80 bps rise in the 10-year yield will likely push cap rates higher across all property types, lowering commercial real estate values.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A rate surge that proves lasting rather than temporary, or a larger and longer cap rate repricing than expected.

theme_stances.key_argument: The rate-driven selloff created valuation opportunities in high-quality names with strong organic growth.
theme_stances.evidence: outlook for U.S. REITs remains constructive on a 12-month horizon

theme_stances.key_argument: The market should reward earnings visibility and internal growth over external acquisition-dependent models while rates stay elevated.
theme_stances.evidence: reward earnings visibility and internal growth over external acquisition-dependent models

theme_stances.key_argument: The gap between strong Japanese real estate fundamentals and weak share prices should narrow as 2Q26 results come in.
theme_stances.evidence: The sharp contrast between real estate fundamentals in Japan and share price performance
